title: Ethical Hacking
overview: Students examine how security weaknesses arise in computing systems and how to recognize, assess, and address them. Lectures and controlled virtual-machine labs connect security principles to defensive decisions and responsible professional practice.
topics: Cybersecurity foundations, authentication, and privacy
Network, system, web, and database security
Malware and social engineering risks
Firewalls, intrusion detection, and network protection
objectives: Assess security weaknesses and propose safeguards for a given network scenario.
Explain how security controls reduce risk and when to use them.
Develop and communicate a network protection plan.
practice: Assignments, controlled labs, quizzes, and exams build applied security judgment. CS 509 students also complete a graduate research project, communicating their findings through a technical report, an oral presentation, or both.

title: Digital Forensics
overview: This course develops the mindset and foundational skills needed to investigate digital incidents. It covers forensic methods for desktop and mobile systems, emphasizing the relationship between technical evidence and legal considerations.
topics: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability
Digital investigation methods and legal considerations
Digital evidence acquisition and media analysis
Forensic tools for desktop and mobile platforms
objectives: Explain core digital forensic methods and relevant legal concerns.
Acquire and analyze basic digital media evidence in a controlled setting.
practice: Hands-on assignments and labs complement a practical investigation project and presentation. Quizzes and exams assess understanding of the methods.

title: Cyber-Physical Systems
overview: Students study computing and communication in systems that interact with the physical world. Using examples such as connected devices, smart grids, and autonomous vehicles, they learn to model, simulate, and verify cyber-physical systems.
topics: Cyber-physical systems and the Internet of Things
Mathematical modeling and simulation
Analysis, testing, and verification
Automatic synthesis and control
objectives: Model and simulate basic cyber-physical systems.
Compare approaches to analysis, testing, and verification.
Explain the role of synthesis and control in cyber-physical systems design.
practice: Students complete an applied project, a short written report, and a virtual poster that describes the motivation, approach, and results.

title: Security in Cyber-Physical Systems
overview: The graduate counterpart to CS 431 connects modeling and analysis of cyber-physical systems to security research. Students examine how to assess systems that combine computation, communication, and physical processes and communicate what their evidence supports.
topics: Cyber-physical systems and the Internet of Things
Mathematical modeling and simulation
Analysis, testing, and verification
Automatic synthesis and control
Current research in cyber-physical systems security
objectives: Apply modeling, simulation, and verification concepts to cyber-physical systems.
Critically evaluate research on cyber-physical systems security.
Communicate security research findings to technical and nontechnical audiences.
practice: Students complete a graduate-level project, write a technical report covering the problem, prior work, methodology, and results, and deliver an oral presentation with slides.

title: Wireless and Network Security
overview: This course covers the security of distributed systems and wired and wireless networks. Students learn to evaluate protocols, design appropriate controls, and reason about the resilience and operation of networked systems.
topics: IEEE 802.11 security, wireless encryption, and authentication
Network key management, routing, switching, and segmentation
Intrusion detection, security monitoring, and denial-of-service resilience
Secure network architecture, incident response, and recovery
objectives: Explain security mechanisms for distributed and wireless systems.
Compare authentication, encryption, and key-management approaches.
Assess network security risks and propose detection, response, and design improvements.
practice: Applied assignments and a course project connect protocol and network design decisions to practical security scenarios. Quizzes and a midterm assess understanding.

title: AI Safety and Society
overview: This honors seminar examines AI safety as a societal and ethical challenge. Students explore how AI risks arise, who is affected, and how governance can protect individuals and communities while supporting beneficial uses.
topics: Machine learning and large language model fundamentals
Societal and catastrophic risks from advanced AI
Transparency, robustness, and unintended behavior
Machine ethics, collective action, and international governance
objectives: Identify and explain major ethical and societal AI risks.
Use ethical frameworks to evaluate competing values and decisions.
Develop practical governance proposals that address AI safety challenges.
practice: Team case studies, discussions, reflective essays, and quizzes build understanding. Collaborative projects develop policy proposals or ethical frameworks for managing AI risks.

title: Ethics, Safety and Security in Computing and AI
overview: This cross-listed course examines ethical, safety, and security decisions in computing and AI. Students evaluate technical and policy evidence and practice communicating their conclusions to technical and nontechnical audiences.
topics: Professional responsibility, fairness, privacy, and stakeholder perspectives
Societal and catastrophic AI risks, reliability, and explainability
Common AI security failure modes, risk assessment, and defensive safeguards
AI governance, standards, regulation, and professional communication
objectives: Identify and analyze ethical, safety, and security risks in AI systems.
Apply ethical reasoning and assess possible controls for AI incidents.
Develop and communicate governance proposals grounded in technical and policy evidence.
practice: Students analyze cases, complete homework and structured lab activities, and work on a collaborative project about an AI ethics, safety, or security challenge.
